content.title: Where is Artemis II splashdown? Will crew be in SoCal after landing?
content.text: April 10, 2026, 7:02 a.m. ETAfter a record-setting journey in space, the Artemis II crew is expected to splashdown off the coast of San Diego on Friday, April 10.Among the buzzy moments of the Artemis II mission: Four astronauts — including a California native — “set the record for the farthest distance from Earth traveled by any human,” according to NASA. That’s on top of them viewing a solar eclipse in space, and the many mesmerizing photos folks back on planet Earth have been treated to thanks to NASA.But the 10-day mission is reaching its end. Here’s what to know about the splashdown.When will Orion splash down?The astronauts are in the middle of a four-day journey back to Earth, using our planet's gravity to naturally "slingshot," or pull Orion back home, negating the need for propulsion or much fuel.The Orion capsule is due Friday, April 10, to reenter Earth's atmosphere to make a water landing around 5:07 p.m. PT in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, California.NASA did not respond to a question about how far off San Diego’s coast the splashdown is expected to occur by the time of publication.Within two hours after splashdown, the crew will be flown to the USS John P. Murtha, which is serving as the recovery ship before the astronauts return to shore to board an aircraft headed to the Johnson Space Center in Houston, according to NASA and the U.S. Navy.Jesus Uranga, a public affairs officer with the U.S. Third Fleet, said the ship will be positioned anywhere from 50 to 100 miles off the coast in a westerly direction. He said it’d be difficult for people to see from land. The astronauts will be taken to Naval Air Station North Island, which is among the facilities that make up Naval Base Coronado.Orion to make parachute-assisted landing near CaliforniaOnce Orion blazes through Earth's atmosphere, the protective heat shield will be cast off to make way for parachutes to deploy and slow the vehicle down.First, two smaller drogue parachutes that are 23 feet in diameter will unfurl at an altitude of 22,000 feet to slow the capsule from about 25,000 mph to 307 mph, according to NASA. Next, three small 11-foot-wide auxiliary parachutes, known as pilot chutes, will be used at about 9,500 feet to ultimately make way for the release of the final three main parachutes at 6,000 feet.Those giant 116-foot-wide main parachutes are to slow Orion from about 130 mph to just 17 mph before the spacecraft lands in the Pacific Ocean.Will you be able to see Artemis II return in California? One expert says soA UC San Diego Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering faculty member reportedly told UC San Diego Today that people along the Southern California coast “should look west over the Pacific around 5 p.m.”“Orion will come in fast and low, appearing as a bright streak for less than a minute before splashdown,” Aaron Rosengren said, according to UC San Diego Today.Florida Today, which is part of the USA TODAY Network, spotlighted several instances in which a space-related splashdown was spotted streaking across the sky.Where can I watch the Artemis II mission splashdown?The good news is that there will be many ways to watch the Artemis II crew return live.According to NASA, your options include:Amazon PrimeHBO MaxNASA+NetflixPeacockYouTubeTODAY Californian will be streaming the splashdown on its YouTube page as well.Will there be watch parties for the Artemis II mission splashdown?Californians looking to watch the splashdown with their community can take note of just a few watch parties occurring statewide:San Diego Air & Space Museum is throwing a family pajama party as part of its watch party plans. The splashdown viewing kicks off at 4 p.m., and the event is included with admission.Hotel del Coronado’s Sun Deck will “transform” into the Moon Deck for an Artemis II Splashdown Watch Party beginning at 4 p.m. The hotel said on its Facebook page it’ll have a specialty cocktail called “The Splashdown.”The Columbia Memorial Space Center in Downey is hosting a free watch party starting at 4 p.m., according to its website.The USS Hornet Museum in Alameda is hosting a watch party of sorts. The museum will play NASA coverage during its regular hours of 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Depending on NASA’s schedule, the museum will stay open late to show the splashdown, according to the museum.The Chabot Space & Science Center in Oakland is hosting a splashdown party from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. The event, free with the cost of admission, will feature experts from NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley and a viewing of the splashdown, among other activities, according to the center.USA TODAY Network reporter Eric Lagatta contributed to this story.Paris Barraza is a reporter covering Los Angeles and Southern California for the USA TODAY Network. Reach her at pbarraza@usatodayco.com.
